newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish government says strike turnout feeble.
newsitem.headline: Spanish government says strike turnout feeble.

text.p: Spain's conservative government said only one in five civil servants had heeded a call for a walk-out on Wednesday in protest against a wage freeze aimed at helping the country qualify for Europe's single currency.
However unions, who called two million civil servants to stop work for 24 hours in protest against a freeze on their 1997 salaries, said turnout was about 80 percent.
"The government has calculated that between 18 and 20 percent of civil servants have gone on strike," a senior government source told Reuters.
If accurate, the government's figures would make the stoppage one of the least successful in recent years.

Tens of thousands of workers also took to the streets in regional capitals to protest against the wage freeze which the government says is vital to trim its 1997 budget in the runup to Europe's planned monetary union.
In Barcelona, police said more than 100,000 demonstrated, some throwing oranges and eggs at government buildings. About 5,000 protested at the wage freeze in Madrid, police estimated.
Trade unions warned on Tuesday the strike would strip hospitals, schools, postal services, courts, public television stations and airports of a large percentage of their staff.
But early estimates from the government put the figure at around 15 percent. It later rose to more than 18 percent.
"There is absolute normality. Transport, schools, hospitals and public services are all working," chief government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez said.
However the deadlock looked set to persist with unions vowing on Wednesday to keep up the fight against the government's tough budget plan.

"If the government maintains its closed and obstinate attitude, refusing to move even an inch, we must warn that we will continue industrial action as long as necessary until the problems are solved," said one union leader.
The government reiterated on Wednesday the freeze was not negotiable but said it would be happy to enter talks on wider issues.
The conservative government took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule. It sparked mass protests in July by announcing a freeze on public sector salaries in 1997 in order to trim the budget.

The unions, led by the Workers' Commission (CCOO) and by UGT, say the freeze violates a deal with the previous Socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise next year in line with inflation.

The Popular Party government made an election promise to push Spain into EMU and says the 1997 freeze is an essential part of its austere draft budget aimed at bringing the deficit down to the level required to join the single currency in 1999.
